words.definition: The total amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, produced by a person, organisation or activity.
words.example: Individuals can significantly reduce their carbon footprint by flying less and eating less red meat.

words.definition: To make something harmful or unpleasant less severe or serious.
words.example: Governments must act decisively to mitigate the effects of climate change on vulnerable coastal communities.

words.definition: A decline in the number and variety of plant and animal species in a place or on Earth as a whole.
words.example: The clearing of tropical rainforests for agriculture is one of the principal drivers of biodiversity loss worldwide.

words.definition: Describing energy or resources that come from natural sources, such as wind or sunlight, which are not used up.
words.example: Investing in renewable energy not only cuts emissions but also creates thousands of skilled jobs.

words.definition: To make a problem or bad situation worse.
words.example: Rapid, poorly planned urbanisation has exacerbated air pollution in many developing cities.

words.definition: To stop using or producing something gradually, in planned stages.
words.example: Several countries have pledged to phase out new petrol and diesel cars within the next decade.

words.definition: The cutting down or burning of large areas of forest.
words.example: Deforestation driven by cattle ranching and palm oil production releases vast quantities of stored carbon into the atmosphere.

words.definition: Unable to continue at the same level or rate without causing serious damage or running out.
words.example: Current levels of consumption in wealthy nations are simply unsustainable if every country is to enjoy a similar standard of living.

words.definition: To control or limit something that is harmful or undesirable.
words.example: Stricter regulations are needed to curb emissions from heavy industry and aviation.

words.definition: All the living things in a particular area, together with the environment they depend on and interact with.
words.example: Plastic waste poses a severe threat to marine ecosystems, entangling wildlife and entering the food chain.

words.definition: Impossible to change back to how it was before.
words.example: Scientists warn that some of the damage to the polar ice sheets may already be irreversible.

words.definition: A tax on fuels and products according to the amount of carbon dioxide they release.
words.example: Although a carbon tax may raise living costs in the short term, it forces polluters to pay for the damage they cause.

words.definition: A reduction in the amount of something, so that very little of it remains.
words.example: The depletion of groundwater reserves threatens food security in several arid regions.

words.definition: The protection of plants, animals, natural areas and resources from damage or destruction.
words.example: Conservation efforts are often underfunded, particularly in the developing countries that are home to most of the world's species.

words.definition: The point at which a species is very close to dying out completely.
words.example: Poaching and habitat destruction have pushed many large mammals to the brink of extinction.
collocations: push to the brink of extinction
bring back from the brink of extinction

words.definition: Plastic items, such as straws and carrier bags, that are designed to be used once and then thrown away.
words.example: Banning single-use plastics is a relatively painless way to reduce the volume of waste entering the oceans.

words.definition: The gradual damage to the natural environment through pollution, overuse of resources or destruction of habitats.
words.example: Environmental degradation disproportionately affects the poorest communities, who depend most directly on the land and water around them.
